claims.text: A composition-optimized refractory HEA can provide the high-temperature mechanical stability needed for fusion plasma-facing components.
Selecting refractory elements that produce only short-lived radionuclides will give the HEA low neutron-activation behavior.
Refractory HEAs can be produced by arc melting.
Refractory HEAs can be produced by additive manufacturing.
The initial refractory HEA contains several refractory elements in near-equiatomic ratios.
Tungsten forms long-lived activation isotopes and should therefore be reduced or replaced.
Alternative refractory elements can yield only short-lived radionuclides while preserving high melting points and mechanical strength.
Fusion plasma-facing components must operate at temperatures of at least 1000 K.
Fusion plasma-facing components are exposed to neutron irradiation and intense plasma-induced particle fluxes.
Tailored composition can produce a robust single-phase or dual-phase refractory-HEA microstructure, such as a continuous BCC matrix with discrete precipitates.
The optimized microstructure is achieved through solid-solution strengthening and phase stability.
Elemental selection reduces activation by minimizing formation of long-lived radionuclides under neutron flux.
The multi-principal-element structure enhances high-temperature mechanical performance through solid-solution strengthening and microstructural stability.
The modified refractory HEA will have significantly less long-lived radioactive activation than conventional tungsten alloys.
The modified refractory HEA will retain or exceed the high-temperature mechanical properties of conventional tungsten alloys.
Tungsten is a leading plasma-facing material because of its high melting temperature, low erosion rate, and low tritium retention.
Tungsten-based plasma-facing components suffer from high neutron activation.
Tungsten plasma-facing materials undergo degradation including brittle failure, blistering, pits, holes, and bubbles.
The exact elemental ratios and long-term irradiation behavior under realistic plasma exposure remain undetermined.
Extrapolating laboratory irradiation results to reactor conditions carries inherent uncertainty.
